extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, humor writers, creative entrepreneurs, and readers interested in The New Yorker/cartooning
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for creating and commercializing cartoons in the style of The New Yorker, including aesthetic qualities that make a drawing successful and practical steps for turning cartoon work into a business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interestingness over mandatory laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: “The New Yorker doesn’t call a cartoon a cartoon. The material of interest is referred to as a ‘drawing.’ And because it’s a drawing, not a cartoon, it doesn’t necessarily have to be funny. Interesting is enough.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful New Yorker drawing can prioritize being interesting or thought-provoking rather than producing an outright laugh. Example references: William Steig, Saul Steinberg. Anti-pattern: assuming a loud or obvious gag is required for acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive engagement / reader participation
rubrics_metrics.description: “They made the reader think. You had to be a participant in the experience…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons should engage the reader’s mind — require participation, inference, or recognition. This means crafting work that invites interpretation rather than spoon-feeding a punchline. Scoring note: higher marks for cartoons that reward reader knowledge or inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and cultural literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators should be “up-to-date on the latest trends and buzzwords, aware of the world around you” to make the work resonate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of contemporary references and cultural touchpoints strengthens relevance. Use of current buzzwords or topical contexts can make otherwise subtle drawings land with readers who share that knowledge. Anti-pattern: insular or anachronistic references that alienate the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental flexibility and appreciation of varied comic visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess a “mental flexibility able to appreciate different comic visions, techniques, and talents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to multiple comedic modes (subtle, absurd, ironic, philosophical). Study varied practitioners to incorporate diverse techniques rather than sticking to one familiar mode. Scoring: versatility is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual / subtle humor (Steinberg-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steinberg’s cartoons “didn’t cause an outward laugh… but they made my mind smile. Each one was a philosophical mediation in ink.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor subtle, intellectual, or philosophical humor that rewards contemplation. Such pieces may not elicit an immediate laugh but create a lasting appreciative reaction. Example: cartoons that function as brief meditations or reframings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity via caption-image dissonance (Thurber-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thurber’s captions “didn't make sense of the image. Instead, the caption made what was going on stranger… go-with-the-flow humor in which you enjoyed absurdity by giving yourself over to it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caption/image relationships that increase strangeness or ambiguity rather than clarifying them; allow the caption to alter or complicate the visual scene. This can produce a pleasurable, odd comedic effect. Anti-pattern: captions that merely restate the obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiosyncratic weirdness / originality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Weirdness by definition, if truly weird, needs to be idiosyncratic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original, personal oddness is more valuable than imitation of generic ‘weird.’ Strive for a distinctive voice or sensibility; avoid being weird for its own sake. Scoring favors originality and identifiable authorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and voice can outweigh technical drawing skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Thurber’s “apparent lack of drawing skill… offered a kind of assurance” — drawing ability need not match academic standards for success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong idea, voice, or conceptual framing can compensate for amateurish draftsmanship. Don’t let lack of polished rendering prevent submission; focus on concept and voice. Anti-pattern: overemphasis on technique at cost of idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the publication’s aesthetic by systematic study ('cartoon college')
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankoff educated himself “by spending countless hours at the New York Public Library” studying every single issue since 1925 to understand what made cartoons work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform disciplined, archival study of the target venue’s past work to internalize its tastes and norms. Practical step: analyze many back issues to reverse-engineer recurring themes, formats, and tones. Scoring: submissions showing clear knowledge of the venue’s sensibility score higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rejection as a resource / exploitation of selection scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Yorker receives far more cartoons than it prints (about 500 submitted weekly vs. ~17 printed), so many rejects are still strong; Mankoff’s idea was to use rejects as the Cartoon Bank’s initial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize high rejection rates as opportunity: rejects can find other markets or be repurposed. Entrepreneurial strategy: curate and monetize rejected work rather than viewing rejection solely as failure. Anti-pattern: assuming a reject equals 'stinker' without re-evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine creative, commercial, and technical skills for viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing the Cartoon Bank to life required “an understanding of cartoons, both creatively and commercially, and some computer skills.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful creative entrepreneurship blends craft knowledge with business sense and basic technical ability. Practical guidance: learn licensing models, basic digital tools (scanning, archiving), and market channels. Scoring for projects should consider both artistic merit and commercial/operational feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt appropriate technology for distribution and monetization
rubrics_metrics.description: As scanners and Macs improved, Mankoff stored cartoons digitally, which made selling and distributing them feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage available tech to archive, present, and sell work (scanning, digital catalogs, online licensing platforms). Early adoption and technical savvy can create first-mover advantages. Anti-pattern: ignoring distribution technologies and relying only on traditional print routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect creative integrity when scaling / beware corporate mission drift
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankoff notes the fun stopped when the Cartoon Bank’s focus shifted to promoting Condé Nast’s photos and other corporate content — a shift that warped the venture’s original heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commercializing creative projects, be mindful of how growth or corporate interests may change the mission or audience. Consider exit strategies or boundary conditions (e.g., negotiate terms) to preserve core values. Anti-pattern: allowing platform owners to repurpose creative channels solely for unrelated corporate promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate terms and roles when selling or partnering
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankoff agreed to sell the Cartoon Bank on two conditions — that he remain president and be made cartoon editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relinquishing or monetizing an idea, negotiate conditions that preserve creative control, leadership role, or mission alignment. Practical tip: identify non-negotiables before pitching and secure them in agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence, tenacity, and reframing rejection as a springboard
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankoff’s career is presented as a “testament to the power of self-education, tenacity, and the gift of seeing rejection not as a deterrent but as a springboard for entrepreneurship.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term success often arises from persistence, study, and reimagining setbacks as opportunity. For creators, this includes continuous practice, iterative submission, and finding alternate outlets for work. Scoring: demonstrated persistence and adaptive responses to rejection are positive indicators.
